results.account: I am Tajōmaru, and men may name me thief, but no man living may name me coward or common cutthroat. It is true I took the woman before her husband's eyes; it is true that, having taken her, I meant to leave the two of them their lives. But she would not have it so, weeping that she could not live having been looked upon by two men, and that one of us must die before she would follow the other. To cut down a man bound and helpless against a tree is the work of a butcher, not a warrior, and with such work I would not stain myself. So with my own blade I severed the ropes that held Takehiro to the cedar, set steel again in his hand, and bade him rise and meet me as a samurai. Three-and-twenty times our swords crossed in that grove — mark it well, for no other man has stood so long against me — until I struck the longsword from his grip and it fell clean among the leaves. I bore him down, and because a beaten warrior deserves a swift death and not a slow butchering, I took up the small dagger and gave him one deep stroke to the throat, as a man honors a fallen enemy. His longsword I left unstained upon the ground, for it was never that steel which ended him, and the woman, when I turned to seek her, had already fled away through the bamboo. Then I too went from that place — a bandit, if you will have it so, but one who freed his enemy, fought him fairly, and killed him with honor.

They call me a cutthroat; hear, then, how a cutthroat conducts himself. I drew the samurai and his wife into the grove with word of a fine old sword lying buried among the roots, for I take my men by wit before I take them by force. I bound the husband to the cedar and lay with the wife before his eyes, and I will not whisper it, for a man who fears to be seen is only half a man. When it was finished she would not be still, saying that two living men who knew her shame were one too many, and that she would follow whichever of us remained. I am no coward to open the throat of a bound prisoner; with my own hand I cut the ropes and stepped back to offer him steel and an honest death. Yet he never raised his blade to mine — it was the small dagger that found his throat, her dagger, not the long sword at my hip, which you will find as clean as the morning frost. I looked once on what the two of them had wrought between them, then left the woman her life and the grove to its silence, for I had come there for a sword, and I do not linger to be any widow's second husband.

Yes, I took the woman, and I deny none of it — I have never been ashamed of what my hands have done. But how the man came to die is a thing I will not have twisted in the telling. When it was finished, she pressed herself to me and said she could not live while two men breathed who had seen her disgrace; one of us must fall, and she would go with whoever remained. I am no cutthroat to open the throat of a bound and helpless man and call it a killing — that is the work of vermin, and I would sooner die than wear the name. So I cut the ropes from the cedar, put a sword in his hand, and let him stand as my equal; three-and-twenty times our blades crossed before mine ran him through. Few men have held against me so long, and I tell you plainly he met his end like a warrior. When it was done the woman had vanished, and I did not give chase — I am a man who takes what he will, not one who runs after what has fled. Bind me, behead me, do as you please; I have spoken it all, and I take back nothing.

When the bandit had taken his pleasure and gone from the grove, the first thing I sought, lying among the trampled leaves, was my husband's face. I had thought to find grief there, or pity, or even an anger that might have consoled me — but his eyes held only a cold and steady loathing, colder than any word he could have spoken. I have borne much in my life, yet that gaze I could not bear; a woman so looked upon is already half dead. I rose and took up the small dagger that had fallen in the grass, and I said to him that since I had been so shamed, I could not leave him living to despise me — that we would go together, and I would follow him at once. With my own hand I cut the rope that bound him to the cedar, so that he need not die trussed like a beast. Then, scarcely knowing myself, I drove the blade once into his throat, and he made no sound. Afterward I meant to turn the dagger upon my own breast and go with him; I tried, and tried again, but my strength failed me and death would not come. I do not ask to be thought blameless — only to be understood: I killed the man I loved because I could not live beneath his scorn, and of all my sorrows I am most ashamed that I am still alive.

When the robber had worked his will and gone from us, I lay in the crushed bamboo grass with my sash undone, and for a long while I could not raise my face. At last I crept to my husband and cut the cords that bound him to the cedar, thinking that we would weep together as those who had shared one life. But in his eyes I found no sorrow and no pity, only a cold and unmoving contempt, as though the shame were mine alone and I had betrayed him. That look wounded me more deeply than the man had done, and I sank down senseless before it. When I came to myself I understood that a wife so regarded cannot go on living, and that a husband so disgraced ought not to be left behind. I told him then that our honor was lost, and that we must go together into death, and in his silence I believed I read his answer. With the small dagger that was my own I pierced his throat but once, and he did not turn away from the blade. Afterward I set that same edge against my breast, and sought the pond, and every road that leads out of life, but I am only a weak woman, and death would not have me. I do not come before you to be called blameless; I ask only that you look with mercy upon one who chose to die, and was refused even that.

When the bandit had taken his pleasure and gone from the grove, I lifted myself from the trampled grass and turned my eyes to my husband. I had looked for grief there, or fury, or even some small pity; what met me instead was a cold and unmoving contempt, as though I had become something unclean that he could no longer bear to see. That look wounded me more deeply than any harm done to my body. I understood then that neither of us could go on living, not he in his loathing, nor I beneath his eyes. So I took up the small dagger and cut the rope that bound him, that he might die as a free man and not as a beast lashed to a tree. I told him we would go together, and to this day I cannot say whether the sound in his throat was consent or refusal. Once only I drove the blade into his throat, and he did not struggle against me. Afterward I tried many times to follow him, upon that same blade and into the still water, but each time my hand betrayed me, and I remain alive, which is a heavier sentence than any death. Do not think me a woman who killed without love; I took the life of the husband I honored because I could not endure to be despised in his eyes.

Hear me, for the dead have no cause to lie. The bandit, having worked his will upon my wife beneath the cedar where I sat bound, spoke soft words to her and bade her follow him wherever he should go. Then she turned upon me a face I did not know, and pointing, said that I must be killed, for she could not belong to two men who had witnessed her shame. Even the robber went pale at this; he threw her to the ground and asked whether he should cut her down for my sake, and for that alone I could almost have pardoned him. While I faltered, she fled into the thickets, and he severed my ropes and departed without a backward glance. Then silence fell, and I found the small dagger gleaming in the trampled grass. I took it up in my own two hands, and knowing that no shame can touch a man who chooses his own hour, I drove it deep into my throat. No enemy's blade undid me; see how the long sword lies unbloodied in the leaves. I died by my own will, and by that will, and not as any helpless thing, I would be remembered.

I will not have it said that I died as a beast is slaughtered, trussed and bleating. When the bandit had spent his cruelty and turned to court my wife with soft promises, I watched her face change, and heard from her own mouth the words that killed me before any blade did: that one of us must die, and it must be I. Even the robber flinched at that; he threw her to the ground and asked me, half in horror, whether he should cut her down, and in that moment, bound though I was, I found I could forgive him more easily than her. She broke free and fled into the shadows, and he cut the ropes from my body and left the grove without once looking back. Then I stood alone in the trampled grass, a free man again, and my freedom left me only one honorable use. I took up the small dagger she had let fall, set its point beneath my chin, and drove it into my throat with a steady hand. There was no struggle and no cry, only the warmth running down and a great stillness rising about me like dusk over the mountains. Let it be known that my longsword stayed clean because I did not deign to raise it; I fell by my own will and no other's, and a man who chooses the manner of his death has not been conquered.

Hear me now, for the living have already begun to lie. When the bandit had worked his violence, he knelt and beckoned my wife to follow him, and she turned her face to me with a light in her eyes I had never seen in all our years, and spoke words I will carry into the dark unrepeated. Even the thief was struck still; he threw her down and asked whether he should cut her throat, and for that mercy I forgave him nearly everything. But she broke free and fled into the bamboo, and he severed my bonds and went out from the grove without a backward glance. Then I was alone, and the small dagger lay gleaming upon the trampled grass. I took it up in my own hand and drove it deep beneath my chin, for a man so unmanned may still command the hour of his own going. No enemy felled me; I fell by my own will, and in that last deed I was a samurai again. Afterward some stranger crept near and drew the blade from my throat, but I had already passed beyond his reach, and beyond my shame.

I will not deny what I did; I took the woman there in the grove, before her husband's eyes, for I have never wanted a thing and hidden the wanting of it. Yet understand me well — I am no jackal to open a bound man's throat and call that a killing. When the woman said, through her tears, that she could not go on belonging to two living men, and that one of us must fall, I judged the demand a just one. So I drew my blade and cut the cords that held him to the cedar, and I gave him back his own long sword, for I would face a samurai standing, not trussed like a beast. We crossed steel three-and-twenty times among the roots, and I will say plainly that no man before him ever stood against me so long. At the last we closed and went down together, grappling, and the swords lay useless beside us, ringing upon the earth without ever drawing blood. There my hand found the small dagger among the leaves, and I set it once into his throat, deep, and in a single breath the thing was done. When I rose, the woman had already fled the grove, and I did not lower myself to hunt her through the trees. I took up the long sword again, clean as the morning, and walked out the way I had come — a man who has killed, yes, but who killed fairly, face to face.

Yes, it was I who drew them into the grove with talk of an old sword, I who bound the husband to the cedar and took the wife before his eyes; I have never troubled to deny what I have done. But hear me: I am no cutter of bound men's throats, for there is no honor in slaughtering the helpless. When the woman, shamed past bearing, cried out that one of the two men must die, I would not play the coward and butcher one who could not so much as lift a hand. So I drew my blade and cut the ropes from the cedar, and offered Takehiro his longsword, that we might settle the matter as men. Yet the samurai, hollowed by the shame of all he had watched and not prevented, could not bring himself to raise it against me. He took up the small dagger his wife had let fall and drove it deep into his own throat, and so his long blade went home unbloodied. I do not kill what will not fight; I turned my back on that place and left the woman her life. Remember me, then, as the man who gave his enemy a fair chance to die upon his feet, and not as a thief skulking in the reeds.

I will not deny what the grove already declares against me: I drew them in with talk of an old sword buried in the hills, bound the husband to the cedar, and took the wife before his eyes. Yet hear how the man came to die, for on this the ground itself bears me honest witness. When it was done, the woman rose and said she could not live so shamed between two men, and that one of us must not leave the grove alive. I am no cutthroat, to open the throat of a bound and helpless man; such a killing would have disgraced me forever. So with my own hand I cut the ropes from the cedar and bade him take up his blade against me. He rushed me as a samurai should, and we closed and grappled; and though he was armed, I bore him to the ground, caught up the small dagger that lay between us, and drove it once, deep, into his throat. My long sword I never drew, and it stayed clean, for no lesser swordsman is worth the trouble of it. The wife I did not touch again, and she was living still when I rose and walked out of the grove. Set it down so: Tajōmaru freed his enemy before he faced him and gave him an honest death, never a coward and never a common thief.

When the bandit had taken what he wished and gone out from the grove, I was left kneeling in the trampled grass, my little dagger fallen at my side. I crawled to my husband, still lashed to the cedar, and lifted my face to his, hoping to find some tenderness that might let me go on living. Instead his eyes held a light I had never known in them, not grief, not anger, but a cold and unbearable contempt. In that gaze I understood that the woman he had loved was already dead to him, and that I could not live on beneath such a look. So I took up the dagger and cut the cords that bound him, for I would not have him die trussed like a beast. Then, with a resolve I mistook for courage, I set the blade to his throat and drove it deep but once, that we might both cross over and be cleansed together. His long sword I never touched; it lay clean among the leaves while the small dagger did its terrible work. Afterward I turned the point upon my own breast, and cast myself toward the pond, and sought a noose from the branches, yet some cruelty would not let me die, and I walked out of that grove alive, when it was death alone I had begged for.

When the bandit had done his will and gone from the grove, I crept to where my husband sat bound, longing for some comfort in his eyes. Instead I met a look I shall never forget — not grief, not tenderness, but a cold and bottomless contempt, as though I were the thing made worthless. That gaze wounded me more deeply than any violence had, and in it I understood that we two could no longer go on living. I cut the cords that held him, for I would not have him die trussed like a beast, but freed, as the man he was. I told him we must pass together into death, and though he spoke no word, his eyes did not refuse me. With the small dagger I ended it at his throat, a single stroke, and his blood was warm upon my hands. Then I turned the blade against my own breast, and again and again I meant to press it home — but my arm had no strength, and the grove would not grant me the death I begged for. I have fainted and waked I know not how many times since, and still I live, I who wished above all to die. If shame there be in me, let it be weighed against my sorrow; I acted not from wantonness, but from a grief that left no other road.

When the bandit had worked his will upon me and gone from the grove without a backward glance, I was left kneeling alone in the trampled grass. I crept to my husband, longing for a single word of comfort, but in his eyes there was neither grief nor tenderness — only a cold and unbearable contempt. That look wounded me more deeply than any cruelty the bandit had done. I understood then that I could not go on living beneath such a gaze, and that he, having witnessed my shame, could no longer wish to live either. Taking up the small dagger that lay fallen among the leaves, I cut the rope that bound him to the cedar, so that he need not die trussed like a beast. Weeping, I begged him to enter death together with me, and in his silence I believed I read consent. My hand did not falter; I set the blade to his throat and gave him the release I thought we both desired. Afterward I sought again and again to follow him, turning the blade upon myself and casting my body toward the pond, yet death would not receive me — and so I am left here, alive and unforgiven, to lay this account before you.

Hear me, for the dead have no cause to lie. When the bandit had worked his outrage, he cut the cords that bound me to the cedar — whether from pity or from contempt, I could not tell. My wife had already fled into the shadows, and the man himself passed out of the grove, leaving the longsword lying clean and untouched upon the fallen leaves. I sat a long while in that silence, and found no enemy left for my hand to strike. Yet a shame had entered me that no blade of another man could ever answer. So I took up the small dagger from where it had fallen, and with a steady hand I drove it once into my throat. No one compelled me; I alone chose the hour and the manner of my going. Remember me, then, not as a beast that is bound and slaughtered, but as a man who, to the last, kept the one thing that was still his own — his will.

Hear me, for the dead have no cause to lie. When the bandit had worked his outrage and gone, my wife knelt and with trembling hands cut the rope that bound me to the cedar, then fled weeping into the trees. Freed, I did not reach for my longsword, for there was no enemy left to strike, and steel turned against a fleeing shadow earns no honor. The shame of that grove fell not upon my hands but upon my name, and a man of my station does not live on beneath such a stain. So I took up the small dagger that lay fallen in the grass, and with a steady will I set its point to my own throat and drove it deep. No man bound me to that death; I chose it, as a samurai chooses, unflinching and alone. Let it be told that I died by my own hand and my own resolve, not as a beast trussed for the slaughter, but as a man who ruled the hour of his going. The longsword I never drew; the dagger did its single, honest work; and the silence that came after was mine to command.

I speak now through this borrowed voice, and I will have the truth stand where my body fell. The bandit, having worked his violence upon my wife, spoke honeyed words and begged her to go away with him; and she, pale as I had never seen her, consented, then turned and said, kill my husband. Even that robber recoiled at her words, and cast her to the ground, and asked me with his eyes whether such a woman should be suffered to live. In that moment she tore free and vanished into the bamboo, and he did not pursue; he cut the rope that bound me and left the grove without once looking back. My longsword lay unbloodied in the grass, for bound to the cedar I had been given no chance to raise it against him. Yet now I was alone, and unbound, and no other hand was upon me; whatever followed would be mine alone. I took up the small dagger my wife had let fall, and though my fingers trembled I did not falter; I set its point beneath my chin and drove it deep into my throat. I welcomed the dark as a man welcomes sleep after long labor, dying by my own will, in honor, and shamed by none but the living.

I am Tajōmaru, and never once in my life have I cut down a bound man, for that is the work of common cutthroats and not of me. When I had taken the woman, she clung to me and said she could not go on living shamed before two men, that one of us must die, and that she would follow whichever of us remained. I would not butcher a helpless captive, so with my own hand I cut the ropes that bound Takehiro to the cedar and raised him to his feet, meaning to grant him an honest death. Yet the man was so unmanned by his wife's words that he would not lift his longsword against me, and I will not pretend that we crossed blades when we never did. A samurai who will not raise his sword has already spoken his choice. So I drew the small dagger, looked him full in the eyes, and drove it once, deep, into his throat, that his end at least be swift and clean. When it was over the woman had already fled through the trees, and I did not trouble to pursue her. I left the grove with his longsword lying clean upon the earth, for it had earned no blood that day. Say of me what you will, but say this also: that Tajōmaru freed his enemy before he faced him, and killed him looking into his eyes.

Yes, it was I who lured them into the grove with talk of an old sword buried among the roots, and I who bound the husband to the cedar. I will not deny the woman; before his eyes I took her, and I am not ashamed to say it. But hear me: I am no common cutthroat who opens a bound man's throat like a butcher at his block. When it was done, I cut the rope from the cedar with my own hand and set the samurai on his feet, for I meant to take his life as one man takes another's. I let him rise to the long sword; he came at me, yet his arm was slow, and his single blow found only air. I would not soil so fine a blade upon so poor a swordsman, so I stepped inside his guard, drew the small dagger, and drove it once, deep, into his throat. He fell without a cry, and the grove went still. Then I walked out unhurried, the way I had come, and left the woman her life — remember me, then, as the man who did this, and not as some skulking thief.

I am no common cutthroat, to open the throat of a man bound helpless to a tree; there is neither fame nor honor in such a killing, and I have never stooped to it. When the woman, her face wet and terrible, cried that she could not go on living while two men who had seen her shame still drew breath, I resolved that the matter would be settled as men settle matters. With my own hand I cut the ropes that bound Takehiro to the cedar and stepped back, that he might take up his longsword and stand against me as an equal. He was a samurai, and like a samurai he reached at once for the blade. But I was the quicker; before his fingers had well closed upon the hilt I was inside his reach, and the small dagger went deep into the hollow of his throat. His longsword never rose and never tasted blood, and it lay clean upon the leaves then as it lies clean now. I left him where he had fallen, and I left the woman with her life, and I walked from the grove at no man's pace, for one who has done nothing beneath him has no cause to run.

When the bandit had worked his will and gone from the grove, only silence remained between my husband and me. I crawled to where he sat bound, thinking to be consoled, but in his eyes I found neither pity nor grief, only a cold contempt that cut me deeper than any violation. I understood then that we two could not go on living with such a thing lying between us. I took up the small dagger from where it had fallen and cut the rope from him, for I would not have a samurai die trussed to a tree like a beast. We were of one mind in that moment, though he spoke no word; his stillness gave me leave. Weeping, I set the blade to his throat with my own hand and sent him before me down the dark road. I had meant to follow, to open my own throat and lie down beside him, but the blade, or this faithless body of mine, would not obey, and so I remain, ashamed to be numbered among the living. Do not think me a woman who kills lightly; I destroyed the one man I loved, and had not even the strength to join him.

When the man had taken what he wished and gone from the grove, I was left alone with my husband, who was still bound to the cedar. I dragged myself to him, weeping, longing for a single word of pity, but in his eyes there was neither grief nor tenderness, only a cold and unbearable contempt. That look wounded me more deeply than any violation, for I understood that in his heart I was no longer his wife but a defiled thing. I took up the small dagger that had fallen upon the grass and cut the rope that held him, so that we might die together as husband and wife rather than live on so shamed. I told him my purpose, and he did not refuse it; his silence I took for consent. Then, scarcely knowing my own hand, I drove the blade into his throat, and he died without a cry. Afterward I meant to turn the dagger upon myself and follow him, yet however many times I tried, my body would not obey, and I remain, to my sorrow, alive. I have wept since in the mountains and the valleys, but grief has not been granted the mercy of death. Judge me as you will; I ask only that you know I struck from anguish and not from hatred, and that I too am a woman who has lost everything.

When the bandit had taken his pleasure and gone from us, he left me kneeling in the trampled grass, and I crawled at last to where my husband lay bound against the cedar. I could not meet his eyes for shame, yet when I raised them I found there neither wrath nor pity, only a stillness that told me we two could not go on living as we had lived. With the small dagger I cut the ropes from his wrists, for I would not have him meet his end tied like a beast. We had no need of words; a wife knows her husband's will, and his will and mine were one, that death alone could wash away what the grove had witnessed. The great sword lay where it had fallen, but such a blade was never meant for this, nor could my hand have lifted it. So I took up the little dagger, and with it I gave him the release we both desired, a single thrust to the throat. Then I turned the blade upon myself, meaning to follow him before the hour was out, but my strength failed me, or some cruel mercy did, and I woke to find myself still breathing and my husband gone before me. I have wandered since beneath the weight of a woman who could not even keep faith with her own death. Judge me, then, not as one defiled who clings to life, but as a wife who did all that a wife was able to do.

Hear me, for the dead have no cause to lie. The bandit took his pleasure of my wife while I sat bound to the cedar, and I bore that shame with open eyes and a shut mouth, for a samurai's strength lies not in his cords but in his spirit. When his lust was spent he poured honeyed words upon Masago, and I watched her face turn from me toward him. She would not meet my eyes; instead she bade him strike me down, and at this even that thief drew back in disgust. They fell to quarreling, and in the confusion he cut the ropes that held me and went his way, leaving me free upon the trampled ground. My wife had already fled, and the small dagger lay gleaming where it had fallen. No other blade touched me that day; my longsword stood clean against the tree, for I crossed steel with no man. I took the dagger up in my own hand, and sooner than live dishonored I drove it deep into my throat. Let it be known that I was not slaughtered but chose my end; the will was mine, and mine alone.

Hear me, for I have crossed beyond all reasons to lie, and gain nothing now by deceit. When the bandit had worked his violence, he sat close beside my wife and poured sweet poison into her ear, and I watched her eyes turn soft toward him. Then she rose, and pointing to where I sat bound, she begged him: slay that man, for I cannot belong to two who have seen my shame. Even the robber paled at such words; he flung her down and asked whether he should kill her or let her live, and in that pause she broke free and fled among the trees, and he chased her, then abandoned the chase and departed the grove — but first he stooped and cut the rope that held me to the cedar. So I was loosed, and I was alone, and the sorrow in me weighed heavier than any cord had. I took up the small dagger she had let fall, and my hand did not tremble; by my own will I drove it into my throat, choosing my death as a man chooses, not suffering it as a beast. No enemy's blade brought me down — my longsword lay clean in the grass, unlifted, unstained, for there was no duel and no hand upon me at the last but mine. Remember me so: not bound, not pitiable, but master of my final breath.

Even now, adrift far from the sun's warmth, I would have my death rightly known, and by whose hand it came. While I lay bound against the cedar, the bandit worked his will upon my wife, and I could do nothing but witness it. Yet when his cruelty was spent, he did not run me through; he stooped, cut the rope that held me, and departed the grove without once looking back. My wife had already fled among the trees, and I was left alone in the trampled grass, the small dagger gleaming where it had fallen. Near it lay my longsword, bright and unbloodied — but no weapon of war could wash away the shame laid upon my name. A man so dishonored does not go seeking an enemy to slay; he answers to himself alone. So I knelt, took the dagger up in a steady hand, and drove it once, deep, into my throat. There was no duel, no thrashing, no cry for rescue — only my own resolve, and the stillness I had chosen. Remember me, then, not as the bound man who looked on, but as the one who, set free, commanded the hour and the manner of his own death.

I am Tajōmaru, and I have never yet struck down an unarmed or a helpless man. It is true I lured them into the grove with the promise of an old blade, true that I bound the husband to the cedar and took the wife before his eyes; a man takes what his strength will allow. But when it was done, the woman said that one of the two men who had looked upon her shame must die, and that she would follow whichever of us lived. I have killed in my time, yet I am no cutthroat to knife a bound prisoner in the dirt: I cut his cords with my own hand and threw him his long sword, keeping for myself only the woman's small dagger. We stood as men before one another, and though he was famed for his skill, his long blade never once touched me; I closed inside his guard and drove the little knife deep into his throat. He fell with a single clean wound, and I will not pretend to you that my hand trembled. When I looked again the woman had fled, so I left him where he lay, his throat opened by that small blade and his own long sword lying clean in the grass. Then I walked out of the grove as I had walked in, alone and in no haste.

I am Tajōmaru, and I have never in my life struck a man from behind. I confess it freely: I lured them with the old sword, bound the husband to the cedar, and took the wife before his eyes — I am not one to hide what I have done. When it was finished, she lifted her face to me and said she could not go on living while two men who had seen her shame still breathed. I am no butcher to open the throat of a man trussed like a beast; I drew my sword and cut his bonds, that he might rise and meet me as a warrior. But when I held the longsword out to him, he would not take it — he closed his own hand upon the small dagger and drove it deep into his throat, choosing the coward's end from which I had freed him. I left him to that end and walked unhurried from the grove, the woman fleeing ahead of me among the trees. Say of Tajōmaru what you will, but say that he feared no man in that grove, and that he killed no bound and helpless man there.

I am Tajōmaru, and I have never once denied what my hands have done. I took the woman before her husband's eyes; I say it plainly, for I have always taken what I wanted. Yet when it was over, she looked from him to me and said she could not go on living, shamed before two men, unless one of us should die. A common cutthroat would have opened the bound man's throat where he sat and been done with it; I am not that kind of man. With my own hand I cut the ropes that held him to the cedar, raised him to his feet, and bade him take up his longsword. We crossed blades many times — I will not name the number — until I struck the sword from his grip and it fell clean upon the earth. He would not yield: he caught up the small dagger from the ground and flung himself upon me, and in that struggle I turned its point into his throat and drove it home once, deep. He died as a warrior should, by the blade and not by the rope, and I gave him that honor. The woman had fled among the trees while we fought, and I did not stoop to chase her. Then I walked from the grove, and this is the whole of it, told without concealment.

The old sword was a lure, and by that promise we were drawn deep beneath the cedars. When the bandit had bound my husband to the tree and worked his violence upon me, I lay in the trampled grass and lifted my eyes to the one gaze that should have sheltered me. But my husband's eyes held neither grief nor anger, only a cold and unbearable contempt, colder than the robber's hands had been. In all my life nothing has wounded me as that single look did. When the bandit had gone from the grove, I crept to my husband and cut the cords that bound him, for I could not bear that we should end as captor's spoil and captive; if die we must, we would die as husband and wife. I whispered that I would follow wherever he went, and in his eyes I read that he consented. Then, with the small dagger, I steadied my hand and gave him a single deep stroke to the throat, and he did not turn his face from me. Afterward I turned the blade against my own breast again and again, by the pond and beneath the trees, yet death would not receive me. So I remain, alive and ashamed to be alive; I beg you, look upon me not as a defiled and broken thing, but as a wife who kept faith with her husband to the very end.

When the man had worked his will and gone from among the cedars, I lay upon the trampled leaves and wished only that the earth would open and take me. I lifted my eyes to my husband, and in his gaze I found no tenderness, only a cold contempt that cut me deeper than any blade. I understood then that we could not go on living, and that death alone might give back what had been torn from us. So I crept to him and severed the ropes that bound him to the tree, that he need not die trussed like a beast. With my small dagger in my hand I begged him, by our silence, to go before me, and I set its point to his throat. His blood was warm upon my fingers, and I meant to follow him in the same breath. Yet when I turned the blade against my own breast my hand would not obey, and again and again I failed to die. How many times I sought my end in that grove I cannot say; I know only that I remain, ashamed to be living, and this is the whole of my confession.

When the bandit had gone at last, I lay a long while among the trampled leaves, unable to lift my face. At last I crept to my husband, and seeing his eyes upon me, I found in them no grief nor tenderness, but only a cold loathing for what had been done to me before him. I understood then that we could no longer live — he in his contempt, and I in my shame — and that death alone might make us clean again. I cut the cords that bound him to the cedar, for I would not have him die trussed like a beast, but as my husband and a man. Then, weeping, I took up the small dagger and pressed it once into his throat; he did not turn from the blade. When it was done I sought to follow him, and set that same dagger to my own breast again and again, yet each time my strength failed me and I could not. The longsword lay untouched in the grass, and I alone was left breathing in that silent place. Let those who hear me judge whether a woman so used had any gentler road; I did only what I believed we both longed for.

I was led into the green shadow by the promise of an old blade, and there the robber bound me to the cedar and worked his will upon my wife while I looked on, my voice lost among the leaves. Do not name me helpless; a man's limbs may be bound, yet his will remains his own. When the deed was done my wife fled deeper into the grove and was gone from sight, and the robber, sated, slashed the rope from my wrists and left me alone beneath the trees. Freed at last, I would not take up my longsword to chase a shadow through the dark, nor carry my dishonor home upon my back. I looked instead to the small dagger lying bright in the trampled grass, and took it up with a steady hand. Better, I judged, to answer shame with my own edge than to go on living as the thing that had been made of me. I set the point beneath my chin and drove it deep into my throat, and the pain was clean, and it was mine alone. The great sword kept its brightness to the end, unbloodied; only the little blade knew my choosing. Remember me, then, not as a man undone by another's hand, but as one who, being freed, chose the hour and the manner of his going.

Through this borrowed voice I speak, for my own breath was stilled beneath the cedars. When the bandit had worked his violence upon my wife, he cut the ropes that bound me and, with a mocking bow, went out from the grove; my wife had already fled among the trees, and I was left alone with my dishonor. A man bound and made to watch such a thing has but one path by which he may become a man again. I saw where her small dagger had fallen upon the trampled leaves, its blade bright and patient in the shadow. With hands still numb from the cords, I took it up, and I did not let them tremble. I set its point to my throat and drove it deep, choosing my own death as a samurai must, that no stranger's hand should ever claim my life. The long sword lay untouched at my side, for such an ending asks not the blade of war but the quiet blade of will. Remember me, then, not as the man who was bound, but as the one who, being loosed, became the master of his own dying.

Through this borrowed voice I, Takehiro, speak at last, and I will have the truth of my death rightly known. The bandit bound me to the cedar and worked his violence upon my wife while I looked on, unable to turn away my eyes. When it was done he asked whether she would follow him, and she, whom I had trusted, bade him first take my life — words that cut deeper than any blade. Yet she fled into the bamboo before he could seize her, and after a time the bandit too went his way, leaving me alive and shamed. Before he departed he slashed the cords that held me, and I sank to the earth a free man in a silent grove. My longsword lay clean among the leaves, for I would not spend my honor chasing a thief or a faithless heart. Instead I took up the small dagger my wife had let fall, and with my own hand I drove it once into my throat. No other man killed me; I chose the hour and the manner of my death, as a samurai may. Let it be remembered that I died by my own will, and not as a helpless thing cast down by another.

Let it be known that Tajōmaru is no cutthroat who butchers a man tied to a tree. When I had taken what I came for, neither shame nor honor — call it what you will — would let me leave him bound and helpless. With my own hand I cut the ropes that held him to the cedar, and bade him rise and defend his wife's name and his own. He came at me with murder in his eyes, and we closed before ever a long blade could be drawn — breast to breast, his strength against mine. In that struggle I laid hold of the small dagger and drove it once, deep, into his throat, and he died as a warrior should, fighting to the last. His fine longsword never tasted blood, for the matter was settled by nearer steel and the stronger arm. The woman I left living, and I walked from the grove at my leisure; I have never yet turned my back on any man. Kill me if you must, but remember me rightly — I set him free, and I met him fair.

Yes, it was I, Tajōmaru, who lured them into the grove with the promise of an old sword, and I will not stoop to deny what these hands have done. I bound the husband to the cedar and I took the wife before his eyes, and I ask pardon for none of it. But hear this: I am no cutthroat to butcher a man trussed like a beast to a tree. When my business was done, I cut the ropes from his wrists with my own hand and set him on his feet, that the matter might be settled between us as men. We fought; and though I might have run him through with my long blade, I scorned to end it so and closed with him instead, until a single thrust of the short blade to the throat granted him a clean warrior's death. I did not touch the woman again, nor take her life; I left her living among the trees and walked back to the road as I had come. Remember me however you will, but remember that Tajōmaru freed his enemy and killed him face to face.

Yes — it was I who drew them into the grove, and I who bound the husband to the cedar; I have never disowned a deed of mine, and I will not begin now. When I had done what I did with the woman, I turned and saw him lashed there, unable to lift a hand, and something in me turned cold at the ease of it. A man of my name does not cut down what cannot cut back; so I took up my blade and cut the ropes through, and bade him stand and settle the matter between us as men. He fought as a samurai should, and the grove rang a long while with our blades, yet I let no edge of mine so much as graze him, for I meant to win clean or not at all. At the last I came inside his guard and tore the long sword from his hands, and with the small dagger I drove a single thrust deep into his throat, that he might die at once, as a warrior dies, and not linger. The woman had slipped away through the thickets while we fought, and I did not hunt her down. I took nothing from him — not the sword, not a coin — but left his arms where they fell. I walked out of that grove as I had entered it, upright and unhurried, fearing no man beneath heaven. Call me robber if you will; no living soul may call me a coward, nor name me the throat-cutter of a bound and helpless man.

When the bandit had gone from the grove, I went to my husband and cut the cords that bound him, that he might not lie trussed like a captive in his last hour. But when his eyes met mine they held no pity, only a cold and unwavering scorn that cut deeper than any dishonor done to my body. It was that look, and not the outrage itself, that made the world no longer fit to live in. I understood that neither a samurai nor his wife could go on breathing beneath such shame, and I read in his silence that he wished for an end as I did. I took up my small dagger, and with a single stroke to the throat I gave him the death we both desired. Then I turned the blade against my own breast, again and again, yet some pitiless fate would not grant me death. How long I lay senseless beside him I cannot say, and when I woke I wandered from that place scarcely knowing I still lived. If I must be judged, let me be judged as a wife who chose to die beside her husband, and was cruelly denied even that mercy.

When the bandit had taken his pleasure and gone from us, I dragged myself to where my husband lay bound against the cedar, seeking some comfort in his face; but in his eyes I found no pity, only a cold loathing that struck me harder than any blow. I had endured the man's violence, yet I could not endure that gaze, which seemed to cast me out from the world of the living. With trembling hands I cut the rope that held him, hoping he might speak one gentle word, but he gave me only silence and that same terrible coldness. Then it came to me that two so shamed could not go on living, and that death alone might wash us clean. I took up the small dagger, and because there was no other road, I drove it once into his throat; he did not turn from the blade, nor lift a hand against me. Afterward I meant to follow him and turn the point upon myself, but my strength failed me again and again, and I sank weeping into the leaves. When at last I woke, the grove was still, and I was, cruelly, alive. Judge me as you will, but know I did not act in hatred; I sought only to die beside the husband I had wronged and been wronged before.

When the bandit had taken what he wished, he vanished among the trees without a backward glance and left us alone. I crawled to my husband, weeping, but in his eyes I found neither grief nor tenderness, only a cold and steady loathing that cut me deeper than any violation had. I understood then that we could not go on living, he in his shame of me and I beneath that gaze. I cut the rope from his body, that he need not meet his death bound like a captive, and I begged him to die together with me. Whether he consented I cannot say, for his eyes never softened; I set the small dagger to his throat and drove it home with all the strength that was left in me. Then I turned the blade against myself, again and again, yet each time my hand failed and the darkness took me before I could follow him. When I woke, the dagger had slipped from my fingers and my husband was already beyond my reach. I have wished a thousand times that I had died there at his side; that I still draw breath is my punishment, and never was my desire.

The bandit lured us into the grove with the promise of an old sword buried among the roots, and I, drawn on by desire for so rare a blade, followed where I should not have gone. When he had bound me to the cedar, I did not cry out nor beg; I held him in my gaze and let him feel a warrior's contempt, though my hands could do nothing. What was done before me I bore with open eyes, for a man does not shut them against his own grief. When at last my bonds were cut and the two of them had gone their separate ways from that place, I stood alone in the trampled grass, and the small dagger lay bright before me. I did not wait for another hand to decide my hour. Taking up that dagger in a steady grip, for my longsword was unfit for so private a reckoning, I set its point against my own throat and drove it home, once and deep. Let it be known that Takehiro was not slain in that grove; Takehiro chose, and by his own will died a man.

Hear me, for I speak now through this borrowed voice, and the dead have no cause to lie. When the bandit's cruelty was spent, he drew his blade across the ropes that held me and left me loosed against the cedar. My wife did not come to me; she fled the grove, and the bandit soon took his own leave. So I was alone, bound no longer, yet fettered by a shame that no cord could equal. I did not wail, nor curse my fortune as a lesser man might. Upon the ground lay the small dagger, and I took it up with a hand that did not tremble. By my own will I set its point against my throat and drove it deep, choosing the hour and the manner of my end. My long sword I left unstained, for such a day was unworthy of a warrior's steel. Let it be known that Takehiro was not slaughtered like a snared beast, but died by his own resolve, a man to the last.

Hear me, for the dead have no cause to deceive. The bandit defiled my wife before my very eyes, and though I was bound to the cedar and could not stir, I neither cried out nor begged; I held him in my gaze and let no tear betray me. When his lust was spent, he cut the cords at my wrists and departed, content to leave me living in my dishonor, a crueler stroke than any sword. But a samurai does not outlive his shame. My longsword lay upon the earth unstained, for no honorable combat had been granted me; and so I took up the small dagger that lay fallen near my hand. With a steady arm I drove it deep into my own throat, choosing the hour of my death as a man chooses it, and not as cattle are felled. Remember, then, that Takehiro died by his own will and kept his honor whole.
